The Aircraft Carrier. A capital warship designed to carry and launch aircraft, representing a revolutionary shift in naval power from battleships to air-based warfare. Emerging as a crucial weapon during the interwar period and reaching maturity in World War II, carriers became the dominant force in naval combat.

The first purpose-built aircraft carrier was HMS Hermes, launched by Britain in nineteen twenty-four. The USS Lexington followed for the United States. But the real transformation came with two pivotal battles. The Battle of the Coral Sea in May nineteen forty-two was the first naval battle where the opposing ships never came within sight of each other. All combat was carried out by aircraft. Then in June nineteen forty-two came the Battle of Midway, which confirmed the carrier's dominance. It was decided entirely by carrier-based aircraft, marking the end of the battleship era.

American Essex-class carriers, built during World War II, proved so durable that many served into the Cold War and beyond. The USS Enterprise, CV-six, became one of the most decorated ships in US Navy history, participating in countless Pacific battles. Carriers require extensive support—escort ships, supply vessels, and fighter squadrons, making them the centerpiece of modern naval task forces. The size and cost of modern nuclear-powered carriers make them symbols of national power. The US Navy maintains roughly eleven active carriers.

The aircraft carrier replaced the battleship as the Navy's most powerful vessel and remains central to modern military strategy and deterrence.
